IndexedDB ?

Structured transactional browser database for application state.
offlinedataresilience
Open full description & implementation guidance

IndexedDB is a distinct capability within Storage & Local Data. Structured transactional browser database for application state. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is durable state, portability and data ownership.

A production implementation should avoid coupling IndexedDB directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include offline-first applications, large datasets, portable knowledge commons, local AI assets. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: schema versioning, transactional boundaries, quota behavior, recovery and explicit export paths. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for IndexedDB; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Store projects, tasks, evidence and preferences locally.

Recommended use

offline-first applications, large datasets, portable knowledge commons, local AI assets

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect IndexedDB through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include silent data loss, incompatible migrations, quota exhaustion and stale duplicate state. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: fall back to simpler browser storage or explicit file export while preserving readable core data. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

i18nglobalaccessibility
Open full description & implementation guidance

RTL support is a distinct capability within Internationalization & Localization. Mirror layouts for right-to-left languages. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is internationalization & localization.

A production implementation should avoid coupling RTL support directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include global communities, cross-border research, education, international institutions. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for RTL support; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Render Arabic navigation correctly.

Recommended use

global communities, cross-border research, education, international institutions

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect RTL support through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include hidden coupling, unsupported assumptions, stale state and difficult recovery. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Recommended contexts include private copilots, prompt improvement, research synthesis, agent-assisted workflows. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. The primary architectural objective is realtime multi-user transport.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Collaborative whiteboards directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include multiplayer workspaces, shared maps, live games, remote workshops. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: transport-independent message schemas, reconnect semantics, admission, presence, backpressure and encryption. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Collaborative whiteboards; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Use Collaborative whiteboards in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Recommended use

multiplayer workspaces, shared maps, live games, remote workshops

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect Collaborative whiteboards through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include NAT failure, peer churn, packet loss, version mismatch and room partition. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: downgrade from peer transport to server realtime or asynchronous local-first synchronization. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is least-privilege protection and verifiable integrity.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Permission dashboard directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include public web apps, institutional deployments, plugin systems, AI-assisted applications. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: threat modeling, strict input/output boundaries, secure defaults, key lifecycle and browser security policy. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Permission dashboard; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Use Permission dashboard in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Recommended use

public web apps, institutional deployments, plugin systems, AI-assisted applications

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect Permission dashboard through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include XSS, privilege escalation, unsafe imports, secret leakage and false assurance. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: disable optional capability, preserve read-only access and surface recovery guidance. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

Web Components is a distinct capability within Modular Application Architecture. Build framework-neutral reusable interface components from browser standards. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is modular application architecture.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Web Components directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include large suites, plugin ecosystems, multi-domain platforms, long-lived projects. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Web Components; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Use Web Components in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Recommended use

large suites, plugin ecosystems, multi-domain platforms, long-lived projects

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect Web Components through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include hidden coupling, unsupported assumptions, stale state and difficult recovery. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: degrade to a simpler explicit workflow while preserving core data and user agency. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

DOM recycling is a distinct capability within Performance Engineering. Reuse DOM structures for very large dynamic lists instead of repeatedly allocating nodes. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is performance engineering.

A production implementation should avoid coupling DOM recycling directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include mobile users, large datasets, AI-heavy apps, global deployments. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for DOM recycling; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Use DOM recycling in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Recommended use

mobile users, large datasets, AI-heavy apps, global deployments

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect DOM recycling through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include hidden coupling, unsupported assumptions, stale state and difficult recovery. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: degrade to a simpler explicit workflow while preserving core data and user agency. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

WebGPU → WASM → JavaScript fallback is a distinct capability within Resilience & Graceful Degradation. Provide progressively slower compute paths rather than treating GPU support as mandatory. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include mission-critical tools, field work, large PWAs, public services. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for WebGPU → WASM → JavaScript fallback; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

The primary architectural objective is installable resilient web-app behavior.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Application URL handling directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include installable tools, offline suites, desktop-like PWAs, field apps. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: service-worker versioning, update UX, cache policy, install diagnostics and platform fallbacks. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Application URL handling; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Use Application URL handling in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Feature-fusion guidance

Identify work that cannot proceed because required tasks, data or approvals are missing.
workflowautomationcoordination
Open full description & implementation guidance

Blocking/dependency detection is a distinct capability within Workflow & Automation Engines. Identify work that cannot proceed because required tasks, data or approvals are missing. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is repeatable coordinated work.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Blocking/dependency detection directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include institutional processes, research review, project operations, agent workflows. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: typed states, explicit triggers, permissions, retries, human approval and audit history. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Blocking/dependency detection; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Example

Use Blocking/dependency detection in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Recommended use

institutional processes, research review, project operations, agent workflows

Feature-fusion guidance

Fusion guidance: connect Blocking/dependency detection through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

Risks & failure modes

Failure modes to design for include automation loops, accidental escalation, stuck jobs and opaque decisions. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: allow manual execution and recovery from the last completed state. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. The primary architectural objective is gamification tied to real work.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Knowledge mastery tracking directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include education, volunteer coordination, community projects, serious games. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

Implementation

Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Knowledge mastery tracking; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

Use Knowledge mastery tracking in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

Main risks include excessive GPU/CPU load, battery drain, jank, motion discomfort, browser/API incompatibility, and visual effects obscuring meaning. Test low-power devices, resize/orientation changes, hidden-tab behavior, interruption, and fallback rendering.

Graceful fallback

Graceful fallback: preserve the same information and controls with simpler CSS/SVG/Canvas rendering, static imagery, reduced particle counts or no nonessential motion; never make a visual effect a prerequisite for core navigation or data access.

Open full description & implementation guidance

SDF and MSDF text rendering is an advanced visual implementation capability within Advanced Visualization. Render crisp scalable glyphs in GPU scenes using signed-distance-field techniques. It should be treated as a composable rendering primitive rather than decoration: define what visual state it owns, how it receives data, how it is started/stopped, how it cooperates with the shared render loop, and what lower-fidelity representation replaces it when unavailable.

A production implementation should keep SDF and MSDF text rendering behind a small visual adapter or scene module rather than mixing rendering code into domain logic. Separate scene state, animation state and domain state. Centralize frame scheduling, cancel work on route changes, feature-detect APIs, expose quality controls, and measure frame time before enabling expensive effects. For live multiplayer or data-driven scenes, consume typed events or snapshots and interpolate visual state locally instead of binding network events directly to frame updates.

Recommended contexts include 3D labels, maps, games, network graphs. Favor deterministic seeds or serializable scene parameters where reproducible visuals matter, and make expensive quality tiers opt-in or automatically adaptive rather than assuming desktop-class hardware.

The meta-prompt runner now works without any language model. Deterministic planning is the default; WebLLM remains an optional local refinement layer.

WebLLM engine ?

The 0.2.82 option is deliberately opt-in. It is included as a compatibility fallback for a currently reported class of WebGPU/D3D12 device-loss failures affecting later WebLLM runtimes on some hardware; it has an older model catalog.

Engine idle.
GPU session fault detected. Repeated requestDevice calls are blocked by the app until you explicitly reset the AI session. If Windows still reports DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED/HUNG afterward, fully restart the browser before retrying.

Reference architecture

Online multiplayer commons stack

A progressive capability ladder: failure should downgrade advanced layers, not destroy the core application.

Capability ladder

  1. Level 0: static/read-only reference
  2. Level 1: local interactive state
  3. Level 2: cloud persistence
  4. Level 3: realtime multiplayer
  5. Level 4: peer-to-peer collaboration
  6. Level 5: AI-assisted collaboration
  7. Level 6: cross-project federation

Data sovereignty & integrity

Portable state, hashes and diagnostics

Export what this workbench knows, inspect local state and verify generated files without implying that a hash establishes authorship.

Workspace summary

Hash a local file
SHA-256 can demonstrate integrity relative to a known digest. It does not establish who authored a file.

      
Zero-Harm / Anti-Inversion
Consequential feature fusion should preserve informed consent, reversibility where feasible, privacy boundaries, accessibility, source provenance, appeal/review pathways and explicit distinction between observed facts, modeled estimates and AI-generated inference.
